meanings.short: Of a state or motion: a small disturbance stays small or dies away, so the system remains close to it.
meanings.long: An equilibrium is stable when a small push leaves the system nearby or brings it back, like a ball at the bottom of a bowl. The opposite is unstable, like a ball balanced on a hilltop.

meanings.short: Of a linear equation with constant coefficients: every solution of its homogeneous equation dies away, so all solutions end up alike.
meanings.long: This happens when every root of the characteristic equation has negative real part. The solution then splits into a transient, which depends on the start, and a steady state set by the input alone.

meanings.short: Of a particle, nucleus, atomic state or vacuum: not decaying, or living far longer than the times that matter here.
Of a state or motion: a small disturbance grows, carrying the system further and further away from it.
meanings.long: A pencil balanced on its point is in unstable equilibrium: the slightest push makes it fall.

meanings.short: Of a particle, nucleus or state: decaying into other things after some time.
Of an equilibrium or a cycle: approached by nearby solutions on one side but left by those on the other side.
Of an equilibrium, or an equation: nearby solutions do not just stay close but actually approach it, or each other, as time goes on.
meanings.long: A centre is stable but not asymptotically stable, since nearby solutions circle it forever; a sink is asymptotically stable.

meanings.short: Unchanged by some swap, reflection or turn; for an expression in two quantities, unchanged when they are exchanged.
meanings.long: A symmetric matrix equals its own transpose: the entry in row i, column j equals the one in row j, column i. A real symmetric matrix always has real eigenvalues and a full set of perpendicular eigenvectors.

origin: Greek orthos, right, and gonia, angle.

meanings.short: At right angles; more generally, of two vectors or functions, having a dot product, or an integral of their product, of zero.
meanings.long: Two functions f and g are orthogonal on an interval when the integral of f times g over it is zero. Sines and cosines of different whole-number frequencies are orthogonal over a period, which is what makes Fourier coefficients easy to find. An orthogonal matrix is one whose columns are perpendicular unit vectors, so its transpose is its inverse.

meanings.short: A number λ for which a matrix turns some non-zero vector into λ times that vector, only stretching or shrinking it.
meanings.long: The eigenvalues of A are the roots of det(A − λI) = 0. For a linear system x′ = Ax each eigenvalue λ with eigenvector v gives a solution v e^(λt), so the eigenvalues decide growth, decay and oscillation. A negative eigenvalue reverses the vector; complex eigenvalues, with complex eigenvectors, give spirals and centres.

meanings.short: A non-zero vector that a matrix only stretches or shrinks without turning: multiplying it by the matrix gives a number times the same vector.
meanings.long: If Av = λv, then v is an eigenvector and λ its eigenvalue. Using eigenvectors as new axes turns a coupled system into separate simple equations.

meanings.short: The sum of the numbers on the main diagonal of a square matrix; it equals the sum of the eigenvalues.
meanings.long: The trace does not depend on the basis used to write the matrix. For a 2 × 2 system x′ = Ax, the trace and determinant together decide the kind of motion near the origin. For a tensor the trace is the matching sum over equal indices.

everyday: Not the verb, to follow or draw a path: here, a number found from a matrix.

meanings.short: An equilibrium point surrounded by closed orbits, so nearby solutions circle it forever without approaching or leaving.
meanings.long: For a linear system the origin is a centre when the eigenvalues are purely imaginary. For a nonlinear system the linear approximation alone cannot decide whether a point is truly a centre.

meanings.short: Of an eigenvalue repeated k times: having k independent eigenvectors. A matrix is complete when all its eigenvalues are.
Of a repeated eigenvalue: having fewer independent eigenvectors than the number of times it is repeated; also called incomplete.
meanings.long: A defective eigenvalue does not give enough solutions of the form v e^(λt); the missing ones contain a factor t.

meanings.short: The moment when two parts that kept exchanging energy stop interacting, so each then evolves on its own.
meanings.long: In cosmology, photons decoupled from matter about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, once atoms had formed and the light stopped scattering off free electrons; that light is the cosmic microwave background. Neutrinos decoupled much earlier, about one second after the Big Bang.

meanings.short: Rewriting a set of linked equations in new variables so that each equation contains only one unknown and can be solved alone.
meanings.long: For a linear system the new variables are taken along the eigenvectors; each then grows or decays at its own eigenvalue. For coupled oscillators the new variables are the normal coordinates.

meanings.short: The state of a system at the starting time, such as its position and speed, which picks out one solution of its equation.
meanings.long: A first-order equation needs one initial condition, a second-order equation two. Without them the solution contains arbitrary constants.

meanings.short: A differential equation together with the starting values that pick out one particular solution of it.
An isolated closed orbit of a system, which nearby solutions spiral towards, or away from, as time goes on.
meanings.long: A limit cycle is a self-sustained oscillation with its own size and period, whatever the starting point, like the beat of a heart. A family of nested closed orbits around a centre is not a limit cycle.

meanings.short: An isolated closed orbit that nearby solutions spiral towards from both sides; 18.03 does not use the name for a repelling one.
meanings.long: A limit cycle is a self-sustained oscillation with its own size and period, whatever the starting point, like the beat of a heart. A family of nested closed orbits around a centre is not a limit cycle.

meanings.short: A point where a quantity becomes infinite or undefined, so the usual equations stop working there.
meanings.long: A differential equation can have a singularity where a solution blows up; in general relativity the Big Bang and the centre of a black hole are singularities, where density and curvature become infinite in the theory.

meanings.short: A point where a function, or one of its derivatives, jumps, has a sharp corner or becomes infinite.
meanings.long: At a phase transition the free energy itself is continuous, but a derivative such as the heat capacity jumps or diverges.

meanings.short: For a linear system, the function that multiplies the transform of the input to give the transform of the response.
meanings.long: For p(D)y = f the transfer function is 1/p(s). It depends only on the system, not on the input; its inverse transform is the weight function.

meanings.short: The factor, depending on scale, by which early-universe physics changes the growth of density ripples of each size.
meanings.long: It multiplies the starting power spectrum to give the one after radiation domination; small scales that entered the horizon early are suppressed most, and hot or warm dark matter suppresses them further.

meanings.short: The size of an oscillation or wave: the largest distance from its middle position, or the number multiplying the sine.
meanings.long: For A cos(ωt − φ) the amplitude is A. In quantum mechanics a probability amplitude is a complex number whose squared size gives a probability.

meanings.short: In quantum mechanics: a complex number whose squared size gives the probability of an outcome, such as a transition or a scattering.
meanings.long: Amplitudes, not probabilities, are what add when there are several ways to the same result, which is why quantum alternatives can interfere.

origin: Greek autos, self, and nomos, law.
everyday: In everyday English autonomous means self-governing; here it means that time does not enter the equation.

meanings.short: Of a differential equation: one in which time does not appear on its own, so the rule for change is the same at every time.
meanings.long: For an autonomous equation dy/dt = f(y), shifting a solution in time gives another solution, and the equilibria are the zeros of f.

meanings.short: A picture of a differential equation: at many points, a short line with the slope the equation gives there.
meanings.long: Solution curves follow the little lines, so the field shows how all the solutions behave without solving anything.

meanings.short: The theorem that, under mild conditions, a differential equation has exactly one solution through each starting point.
meanings.long: For y′ = f(x, y) it is enough that f and its derivative with respect to y are continuous. One consequence: two integral curves can never cross or even touch.

meanings.short: A curve that at every point runs along the direction the differential equation gives there: the graph of a solution.
The matrix of all first partial derivatives of several functions; near a point it gives their best linear approximation.
meanings.long: Near an equilibrium of x′ = f(x, y), y′ = g(x, y), the system behaves like a linear one whose matrix is the Jacobian there, so its eigenvalues decide the type of the equilibrium.

meanings.short: A sum of things each multiplied by a constant, such as 2u plus 3v.
A rule that turns functions or vectors into others and respects sums and multiples, so L(au + bv) = aL(u) + bL(v).
Of several functions or vectors: none of them can be written as a combination of the others.
meanings.long: Two functions are linearly independent when neither is a constant multiple of the other. A second-order linear equation needs two independent solutions to build all the others.

meanings.short: Repeating itself exactly after a fixed interval of time or distance, called the period.
The table of chemical elements in order of the number of protons, arranged so that elements with similar chemistry share a column.
An equilibrium that nearby solutions approach by spiralling inwards, as for a damped oscillation.
meanings.long: For a linear system it happens when the eigenvalues are complex with negative real part.

meanings.short: An equilibrium that nearby solutions leave by spiralling outwards, as for an oscillation that keeps growing.
An equilibrium that nearby solutions approach without turning round it; for a linear system both eigenvalues are real and negative.
An equilibrium that nearby solutions leave without turning round it; for a linear system both eigenvalues are real and positive.
For two solutions y₁ and y₂ of a linear equation, the quantity y₁y₂′ − y₂y₁′; it is never zero exactly when they are independent.
meanings.long: For solutions of the same equation the Wronskian is either zero everywhere or zero nowhere, so checking it at one point is enough. For systems the determinant of a fundamental matrix plays the same part.

meanings.short: Worked out exactly with formulas and algebra, rather than by drawing pictures or by computer.
meanings.long: An analytic solution is a formula; a numerical one is a table of approximate values.

meanings.short: Of a function: equal to its own Taylor series near every point, so it is smooth in the strongest sense.
Of mechanics: built on energy functions, as in Lagrange's and Hamilton's methods, rather than on forces.
The angle that a complex number makes with the positive real axis, measured anticlockwise.
meanings.long: Writing a complex number as r e^(iθ), r is its modulus and θ its argument. Multiplying complex numbers multiplies the moduli and adds the arguments.

meanings.short: The size of a complex number: its distance from zero in the complex plane.
meanings.long: The modulus of a + ib is the square root of a² + b². It is also called the absolute value.

meanings.short: The size of a complex number: its distance from zero in the complex plane.
A first-order equation y′ = p(x)y + q(x)yⁿ, which a substitution turns into a linear equation.
meanings.long: Setting v = y to the power 1 − n makes the equation linear in v, which an integrating factor then solves.

meanings.short: A path of a system that joins up with itself, so the system keeps returning to the same state: a periodic motion.
The general solution of the homogeneous equation, which is added to one particular solution to give every solution of the full equation.
Any one solution of the full equation, input term included; adding the complementary solution gives all the others.
meanings.long: For a linear differential equation the others differ from it by solutions of the homogeneous equation. For a linear system Ax = b, the others are found by adding vectors of the nullspace.

meanings.short: The complex number with the sign of its imaginary part reversed: the conjugate of a + ib is a − ib.
meanings.long: A number times its conjugate is the square of its modulus. The roots of a real polynomial that are not real come in conjugate pairs.

meanings.short: To replace a real problem by a complex one, such as a cosine by an exponential, whose real or imaginary part gives the answer.
meanings.long: Exponentials are much easier to differentiate and integrate than sines and cosines, so the complex problem is solved first and the real answer read off at the end.

meanings.short: Of a curve: bending downwards, so that it lies below its tangent lines; its second derivative is negative.
Of a curve: bending upwards, so that it lies above its tangent lines; its second derivative is positive.
Of a linear differential equation: the numbers multiplying the unknown and its derivatives do not change with time.
meanings.long: Such equations are solved by trying exponentials e^(rt), which turns them into an algebraic characteristic equation.

meanings.short: Fixed numbers multiplying the terms of a series, not changing from point to point.
Damped just enough that a disturbed system returns to rest as fast as possible without oscillating.
meanings.long: For a damped spring the characteristic equation then has a repeated real root. With a strong enough starting push the mass may still cross the equilibrium once.

meanings.short: Damped so strongly that a disturbed system creeps back to rest without oscillating, more slowly than if critically damped.
meanings.long: The characteristic equation has two different real roots, both negative.

meanings.short: Damped lightly enough that a disturbed system oscillates, with a size that shrinks steadily as it settles.
meanings.long: The characteristic equation has complex roots with negative real part, and the motion is a decaying oscillation at the pseudo-frequency.

meanings.short: With no damping at all, so an oscillation keeps the same size for ever.
The number setting how strongly a damper resists motion: the resisting force divided by the speed.
A damper, such as a piston moving through oil, that pushes back with a force proportional to its speed.
meanings.long: A car's shock absorber is one. In the spring–mass–dashpot model it supplies the damping term.

meanings.short: A function defined everywhere by repeating its values on one interval; the even or odd version first reflects it across zero.
meanings.long: The even periodic extension gives a Fourier series of cosines only, the odd one a series of sines only.

meanings.short: Of a function: growing no faster than some exponential, so that its Laplace transform exists.
A first-order linear equation written as y′ + p(x)y = q(x), with the number in front of y′ divided out.
meanings.long: In this form the integrating factor is e to the power of the integral of p.

meanings.short: A differential equation with only the first derivative, in which the unknown and its derivative appear only to the first power, never multiplied together.
meanings.long: Every such equation can be solved with an integrating factor.

meanings.short: A set of equations each giving the rate of change of one unknown in terms of all of them, with first derivatives only.
meanings.long: Any higher-order equation can be rewritten as a first-order system by taking the derivatives as new unknowns.

meanings.short: A set of equations each giving the rate of change of one unknown in terms of all of them, with first derivatives only.
meanings.long: Any higher-order equation can be rewritten as a first-order system by taking the derivatives as new unknowns.

meanings.short: A rule giving each vector in a sequence from the one before it, by multiplying by a fixed matrix A.
A matrix whose columns are independent solutions of a linear system, so every solution is it times a constant vector.
The matrix e^(At), defined by the exponential series with a matrix in place of a number; it solves x′ = Ax.
meanings.long: It is the fundamental matrix that equals the identity at t = 0, so x(t) = e^(At) x(0).

meanings.short: The simplest numerical way to follow a differential equation: step forward along the current slope, find the new slope, and repeat.
meanings.long: Its error is roughly proportional to the step size, so halving the step halves the error: it is a first-order method.

meanings.short: A numerical method that averages the slopes at the start of each step and at Euler's trial end point; also called improved Euler.
meanings.long: Its error is roughly proportional to the square of the step size, so halving the step quarters the error.

meanings.short: A family of accurate numerical methods that sample the slope at several points in each step; RK4 is the standard fourth-order one.
meanings.long: Heun's method is one second-order (RK2) method. RK4 averages four slopes and its error shrinks as the fourth power of the step size.

meanings.short: Equal to zero for every value of the variable, not just at some points.

origin: Greek isos, equal, and klinein, to slope.

meanings.short: A curve along which a differential equation gives the same slope at every point.
meanings.long: Drawing isoclines and putting short lines of the right slope along them is a quick way to sketch a direction field.

meanings.short: The formula for the tiny distance or spacetime interval between two nearby points in terms of their coordinate differences.
meanings.long: In relativity the line element, written ds², is the metric spelled out: for flat spacetime ds² = −c²dt² + dx² + dy² + dz². It contains everything about the geometry.

meanings.short: A short line segment, drawn at a point, with the slope that a differential equation gives there.
A population model in which growth is nearly exponential at first and then levels off at a largest size the surroundings can support.
meanings.long: It reads dy/dt = ay − by², or equally dy/dt = ky(1 − y/M) with M = a/b: the growth rate falls to zero as y approaches M.

meanings.short: A single constant standing for a combination of several, used to make an equation simpler.
The frequency at which a system oscillates on its own, with no damping and no outside force.
meanings.long: For a mass m on a spring of constant k it is the square root of k/m. Driving a lightly damped system near its natural frequency gives resonance.

meanings.short: The rule that a body's temperature changes at a rate proportional to the difference between it and its surroundings.
The two solutions of a second-order equation whose starting value and slope are 1 and 0, and 0 and 1, respectively.
meanings.long: Any solution with starting value a and slope b is then simply a times the first plus b times the second.

meanings.short: How far a response's oscillation falls behind the input's oscillation, measured as an angle.
meanings.long: A response A cos(ωt − φ) to an input cos ωt has phase lag φ; it is also called the phase delay.

meanings.short: An operator built as a polynomial in another operator, such as D² + bD + k in the derivative D, acting on a function.
The rule that the equation p(D)y = e^(at) has the solution e^(at)/p(a) whenever p(a) is not zero.
meanings.long: It turns finding the response to an exponential, sine or cosine input into arithmetic. When p(a) is zero, the case of resonance, a factor t appears instead.

meanings.short: The input frequency that gives the largest response in a damped system, a little below its natural frequency.
The frequency of a damped oscillation, which is not truly periodic because its size keeps shrinking.
meanings.long: It is lower than the natural frequency, and the more damping, the lower it is.

meanings.short: The function that is 0 before time zero and 1 after it, used to switch inputs on.
meanings.long: Shifted to time a, it switches something on at time a; its derivative is the delta function.

meanings.short: A function equal to 1 between two times and 0 at all other times: a step up followed by a step down.
The surprising prediction that harvesting predators and prey at the same rate raises the average number of prey and lowers that of predators.
A linear system's response to a sudden unit kick at time zero; adding up delayed copies of it, weighted by the input, gives any response.
meanings.long: This adding up is the convolution of the weight function with the input. The weight function is the inverse Laplace transform of the transfer function, and is also called the unit impulse response.

meanings.short: A way of turning a function of time into a function of a new variable s, which changes differential equations into algebra.
meanings.long: It is the integral of f(t) e^(−st) from 0 to infinity. Derivatives become multiplication by s, so an equation and its starting values become one algebraic equation for the transform.

meanings.short: A function an equation is multiplied by so that one side becomes an exact derivative; for a first-order linear equation, of a single product.
Ordinary differential equation: an equation linking a function of one variable to its derivatives.
meanings.long: Partial differential equations, by contrast, involve functions of several variables and their partial derivatives.

meanings.short: Of a first-order differential equation: one that can be rearranged with each variable on its own side and then integrated.
A method for an inhomogeneous linear equation that takes the homogeneous solutions and replaces their constants by unknown functions.
meanings.long: For a system x′ = Ax + f it tries x = X(t)v(t), with X a fundamental matrix, which gives v′ = X⁻¹f and so works for any input.

meanings.short: An algebraic equation whose roots give the basic solutions: the rates r in e^(rt) for a constant-coefficient equation, or a matrix's eigenvalues.
meanings.long: For y″ + by′ + ky = 0 it is r² + br + k = 0. For a matrix it is det(A − λI) = 0, whose roots are the eigenvalues.

meanings.short: An electric circuit of a resistor and a capacitor, in which charge flows on or off the capacitor exponentially.
meanings.long: Its time constant is R times C.

meanings.short: An electric circuit of an inductor and a capacitor, in which charge sloshes back and forth at one natural frequency.
An electric circuit with a resistor, an inductor and a capacitor: the electrical version of a damped mass on a spring.
